About 30s.

02

Stellar Scaffold

From idea to working dApp, fast.

A toolkit for full-stack Stellar apps. One command gives you Rust smart contracts, a React, Svelte or no frontend, a local network, and typed TypeScript clients that rebuild every time your contract changes.

  • Scaffold is a toolkit for full-stack Stellar apps.
  • One command gives you Rust smart contracts, a frontend, a local network, and typed TypeScript clients that rebuild whenever your contract changes.

About 20s.

The big idea

Every save rebuilds, redeploys and regenerates your typed client. Spend HackMeridian on your app, not the plumbing.

  • Read the line out.
  • The point: you shouldn't spend the hackathon wiring up builds, deploys and bindings.

About 10s.

The hackathon problem

  • Build Rust → Wasm
  • Deploy, copy the contract ID
  • Generate bindings, paste the ID into the frontend
  • Wire up a wallet and network config
  • …then change one function and do it all again
  • Click through the list as it builds: compile Rust to Wasm, deploy and copy the contract ID, generate bindings and paste the ID into the frontend, wire up a wallet.
  • Land the last line: change one function and you do it all again.
  • This plumbing can eat your whole first day. Scaffold turns it into one loop.

About 30s.

Three things to remember

scaffold.yml = your dependencies

Your app's contract dependencies, per network: what they are and where to get them.

Secrets and machine settings go in .env.

app-lib/clients = generated

A typed client per contract, per network, regenerated on every build and gitignored. Import by name; never paste an address.

Don't edit it: wrap clients under app/.

npm run dev = the loop

Save a contract and it rebuilds, redeploys on the local network, and regenerates its client.

App runs at localhost:5173.

  • scaffold.yml: one file listing your contracts and where each one lives, per network. Secrets stay in .env.
  • app-lib/clients: a typed client per contract, regenerated on every build. Import it by name; don't edit it.
  • npm run dev: the loop. Save a contract and it rebuilds, redeploys locally and regenerates its client.
  • If they remember nothing else from Scaffold, it's these three.

About 45s.

Set up and start a project


cargo binstall stellar-scaffold-cli stellar-registry-cli
# no binstall? cargo install --locked (builds from source)
stellar scaffold doctor   # checks your setup
stellar scaffold init my-app   # react, svelte or none
cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev
    

my-app/
├── contracts/     Rust → Wasm
├── app/           your frontend
├── app-lib/       wallet, network
│   └── clients/   generated
├── scaffold.yml   dependencies
└── .env           local settings
init asks which frontend you want

$ stellar scaffold init my-app
Creating new Stellar project in ./my-app
? Pick a framework ›
❯ react
  svelte
  none (no frontend)

Needs Rust, Node, the Stellar CLI, and Docker. Scaffold and Registry install together as stellar plugins.

  • Install both CLIs. cargo binstall downloads prebuilt binaries, so it's much faster than cargo install, which compiles from source.
  • doctor checks Rust, Node, the Stellar CLI and Docker, and tells you what's missing.
  • init asks which frontend you want: react, svelte or none. Then npm install and npm run dev.
  • Point at the tree: contracts/ for Rust, app/ for your frontend, app-lib/clients is generated, scaffold.yml lists your contracts.
  • Tip for scripts: skip the prompts with --template, -p (package manager) and -y.

About 45s.

Your frontend: React, Svelte or none

Pick react, svelte or none at init. The React and Svelte templates ship wallet connect, network switching, and a working GuessTheNumber component, all using the same generated clients.


import { guessTheNumber } from "@stellar-scaffold/app-lib/clients"   // both
React · GuessTheNumber.tsx

const { address, signTransaction } =
  useWallet()
const tx = await guessTheNumber.guess(
  { a_number: 5n, guesser: address },
  { publicKey: address },
)
await tx.signAndSend({ signTransaction })
Svelte · GuessTheNumber.svelte

import { address, signTransaction }
  from "../stores/wallet"

const tx = await guessTheNumber.guess(
  { a_number: 5n, guesser: $address },
  { publicKey: $address },
)
await tx.signAndSend({ signTransaction })

Only need contracts? stellar scaffold init my-app --template none (or pick none) skips the frontend entirely: no app/, app-lib or generated clients.

  • Both templates ship wallet connect, network switching and a working guess-the-number game.
  • Same client call on both sides; only the wallet plumbing differs: a React hook versus a Svelte store.
  • Only need contracts? --template none skips the frontend entirely.

About 40s.

The loop · 1 of 3

Edit: add a method to the contract

In contracts/guess-the-number/src/lib.rs, next to guess():


/// Is the answer higher or lower than your guess?
pub fn hint(env: &Env, a_number: u64) -> Symbol {
    let n = Self::number(env);
    if a_number < n {
        symbol_short!("higher")
    } else if a_number > n {
        symbol_short!("lower")
    } else { symbol_short!("yes") }
}

hint() is our example, not part of the template. It reuses the template's own Self::number(env), the same helper guess() calls.

  • We'll walk the loop in three slides: edit, save, use.
  • Step one: add hint() to the template's guess-the-number contract. It's our example, built on the number helper the contract already has.
  • That's the whole change: no deploy script, no bindings command.

About 30s.

The loop · 2 of 3

Save: npm run dev does the rest


[stellar] File changed: contracts/guess-the-number/src/lib.rs
[stellar] ℹ️  Changes detected. Rebuilding...
[stellar] ℹ️  Building for network "local" (from `stellar network use`)
[stellar] ✅ Local Stellar network is healthy and running.
[stellar]    Compiling guess-the-number v0.0.2 (contracts/guess-the-number)
[stellar] ✅ Build Complete
[stellar] 🌎 Sending transaction...
[stellar] ✅ Transaction submitted successfully!
[stellar] ✅ Client "guess-the-number" updated successfully

One save: the Wasm rebuilds, the changed contract is updated on the local network, and its TypeScript client is regenerated with hint in it. Contracts you didn't touch stay as they are.

  • Step two: save the file.
  • npm run dev notices, rebuilds the Wasm, redeploys to the local network and regenerates the TypeScript client.
  • Point out the last lines: only the contract you changed is updated; the others are "up to date".
  • This is real output, trimmed: the full log also lists every exported function and each transaction. The very first run also pulls the Stellar quickstart Docker image, so give it a minute once.

About 30s.

The loop · 3 of 3

Use it: typed, in your frontend

In GuessTheNumber.tsx, guessTheNumber. now autocompletes hint:


import { guessTheNumber } from "@stellar-scaffold/app-lib/clients"

const { result } = await guessTheNumber.hint({ a_number: 5n })
console.log(result)   // "higher" | "lower" | "yes"

A read-only call: no wallet signature needed. Same import in the Svelte template.

  • Step three: the method you just wrote in Rust is a typed function in the frontend, with autocomplete and argument names.
  • It's read-only, so no wallet signature.
  • No address and no copied bindings anywhere.

About 30s.

Add a contract


stellar scaffold generate contract --ls   # list examples: stellar/…, oz/…
stellar scaffold generate contract --from oz/nft-royalties   # or --from-wizard
  

contracts:
  my-nft:                   # client name; exported as myNft
    type: workspace         # built from contracts/, deployed locally
    source: nft-royalties   # crate name in its Cargo.toml
    args:                   # constructor args, by parameter name
      uri: https://example.com/nft/
      name: My NFT
      symbol: MNFT
      admin: ${account.me}
      manager: ${account.me}
    networks:               # where your app uses this contract
      local:

stellar scaffold generate writes the crate but does not add it to scaffold.yml; do that yourself.

  • Don't start from a blank file: --ls lists ready-made examples from Stellar's soroban-examples and from OpenZeppelin.
  • --from copies one into contracts/. Then add it to scaffold.yml yourself.
  • Walk the highlights: the key becomes the client name, type workspace means built from contracts/, source is the crate name, args are constructor arguments by name, networks says where it exists.

About 45s.

Go to testnet and ship

By default Scaffold deploys only to your local network. To ship to testnet, publish and deploy with Stellar Registry, then point scaffold.yml at the deployed contract.


contracts:
  my-nft:
    networks:
      local:              # built from contracts/
      testnet:
        type: contract    # already deployed: fetch it
        source: C...      # ID from registry
    

stellar scaffold build --compile-only
stellar registry publish ...  # next talk
stellar registry deploy ...
stellar scaffold build --network testnet
npm run build                 # → dist/

Set STELLAR_NETWORK=testnet in .env. Contracts can differ between networks: make sure the app still typechecks.

  • By default Scaffold deploys only to your local network. You can opt in to more with allow-deploy, but the recommended path to testnet is Registry.
  • The flow: compile the Wasm, publish and deploy it with the registry (that's the next talk), then point scaffold.yml's testnet entry at the deployed contract.
  • build --network testnet regenerates the clients against testnet, and npm run build gives you a static site to host anywhere.

Your contract works locally.
How do you get it onto testnet under a name,
and use other people's without copying addresses?


stellar registry publish …   # under unverified/
  • Read the question out loud.

About 10s.

03

Stellar Registry

Name it. Publish it. Import it.

Scaffold runs your contract locally. The registry is how it gets to testnet: publish the Wasm, deploy it under a name, and anyone, your own app included, uses that name instead of a C… address.

  • Answer the question: Scaffold runs your contract locally; getting it onto testnet under a name is Registry's job.
  • And once it has a name, anyone can find it. You use other people's contracts by name the same way, with no copied addresses.

About 40s.

The big idea

Give your contract a name, not an address. Ship it to testnet, and let anyone use it by that name.

  • Read the line out.
  • A name instead of a C… address: the same name works on every network, and nothing gets pasted into your frontend.

About 10s.

Three things to remember

Wasm = published code

Reusable contract code under a name and a semantic version. Only its author can publish new versions.

unverified/guess-the-number@1.0.0

Contract = deployed instance

A live contract registered by name. The name resolves to its C… address.

No version: it's one address.

unverified/ = open to all

Anyone can publish here, no approval. Bare names on the main registry need a manager's OK.

Use this!

  • Wasm: published code, under a name and a version. Only its author can publish new versions.
  • Contract: a deployed instance. The name points to one address, so it has no version.
  • unverified/: the open channel, no approval needed. Use this!
  • Forgetting unverified/ is the most common error, so say it twice.

About 1 min.

Ship to testnet by name


stellar keys fund me --network testnet
stellar keys use me

stellar registry publish \
  --wasm target/stellar/testnet/guess_the_number.wasm \
  --wasm-name unverified/guess-the-number --binver 1.0.0

stellar registry deploy \
  --contract-name unverified/guess-the-number \
  --wasm-name unverified/guess-the-number --version 1.0.0 \
  -- --admin me                        # constructor args after --

stellar registry fetch-contract-id unverified/guess-the-number   # C… for scaffold.yml

The Wasm is what stellar scaffold build --compile-only wrote with STELLAR_NETWORK=testnet. Add --dry-run to preview any write.

  • Click through the highlights:
  • Fund your testnet account and make it the default.
  • Publish the Wasm Scaffold compiled, under a name and a version.
  • Deploy a named contract from it. Constructor arguments go after the --.
  • fetch-contract-id gives you the C… address you'll put in scaffold.yml.
  • Mention --dry-run to preview any write, and create-alias to call the contract by name from the CLI.

About 1:45.

How names are organised

One root registry, many sub-registries


registry          root: bare names, manager-approved
├── unverified/   open to anyone: use this!
├── oz/           OpenZeppelin Wasms, ready to deploy
├── circle/       circle/usdc
├── soroswap/     soroswap/router, soroswap/factory
├── blend/        blend/pool-factory-v2, …
└── defindex/     defindex/xlm-vault, …

A sub-registry is its own registry contract with its own rules, registered by name in the root. Names read <sub-registry>/<name>.

Sub-registries group related contracts under one prefix, like soroswap/router and soroswap/factory.

Browse them all at rgstry.xyz under Contracts.

  • Every name so far started with unverified/. That's a sub-registry: the open one.
  • The root registry holds bare names, like registry itself, and those need a manager's approval.
  • Other sub-registries group related contracts: oz for OpenZeppelin Wasms, circle/usdc, soroswap's router and factory, blend, defindex.
  • All of them are browsable at rgstry.xyz under Contracts.

About 45s.

Start from OpenZeppelin

Deploy OpenZeppelin straight from oz/


stellar registry deploy \
  --contract-name unverified/my-token \
  --wasm-name oz/ft-standard \
  -- --name "My Token" --symbol MTK --decimals 7 --owner me --initial_supply 1000000

30+ pre-built combinations of OpenZeppelin Stellar Contracts, on testnet and mainnet: ft-standard, ft-capped, ft-pausable, ft-allowlist, ft-votes, ft-vault, nft-standard, nft-royalties, nft-enumerable, …

Your name, their Wasm: deploy into unverified/ from any sub-registry. Want to edit the source instead? stellar scaffold generate contract --from oz/…

  • Need a token or an NFT? Don't write one.
  • oz/ has more than 30 prebuilt OpenZeppelin combinations on testnet and mainnet: fungible tokens with caps, pausing, allowlists or voting; NFTs with royalties or enumeration; vaults.
  • Deploy one under your own unverified/ name. Constructor args go after --, and deploy … -- --help lists them.
  • Want to change the source? Use Scaffold's generate --from oz/… instead.

About 45s.

Call any named contract from Rust

You already have: guess-the-number pays out with stellar_registry::import_asset!("xlm").


let game = stellar_registry::import_contract!(
    env, "unverified/guess-the-number");   // typed client, no address in source

let won = game.guess(&5, &player);
  

STELLAR_NETWORK=testnet stellar scaffold build   # names resolve at build time

Defaults to local, and switching networks rebuilds automatically. Assets like xlm resolve at runtime, so one Wasm works on any network. Contract names resolve at build time: after a redeploy, cargo clean and rebuild.

  • You've already used the registry: the template's guess-the-number imports XLM with import_asset!.
  • import_contract! turns any registered name into a typed client, with no address in your source.
  • Build with STELLAR_NETWORK set; Scaffold's .env does that for you.
  • Asset imports like xlm resolve at runtime, so one Wasm works on any network. Named contracts resolve at build time, so after a redeploy, cargo clean and rebuild.

About 30s.

Registry survival kit

  • Auth failure on publish? You used a bare name. Add unverified/
  • Error(Contract, #5): that contract name is taken. #8: publish a higher --binver
  • Macro can't find a contract? STELLAR_NETWORK wasn't set at build time
  • deploy … -- --help prints the constructor's arguments
  • Teach your agent: Registry skill at skills.stellar.org
  • The errors people will actually hit:
  • Auth failure on publish: you used a bare name, so add unverified/.
  • Error #5: that contract name is taken. Error #8: publish a higher --binver.
  • Macro can't find a contract: STELLAR_NETWORK wasn't set when you built.
  • deploy … -- --help prints a contract's constructor arguments, and skills.stellar.org has the Registry skill for your coding agent.

Nido

Passkey accounts for your app

Nido on the Scaffold Stellar template: what Nido does (5 min), how to Nido (5 min), then questions (5 min).

  • I'm going to show you Nido: passkey accounts for your Stellar app.
  • Five minutes on what it does for your users and your app, five minutes on how to add it, using the Scaffold Stellar template, and then five minutes for your questions.

About 30s.

Sources: github.com/nidohq/scaffold-template (NIDO.md, README.md), github.com/nidohq/scaffold-template/pull/10 (UX walkthrough), stellarscaffold.org/docs/community-templates

New to Stellar?

Stellar has two kinds of account

G-address · starts with G
GBO4H3WFMTNWZU5SJJSXXOW2ML26
TEIQOY66MF2SYANVWAI4JY4YEIJP		 C-address · starts with C
CCH2FDKHAMKNT33JCF6NOOUDKZNF
IKVOM2P5PMDI7D456LLI6VZSO732
What it isAn account with keysA contract
Who can signOne key, or up to 20 with weights and thresholdsWhatever its code allows: passkeys, a G-address, an app’s session key
What it can limitHow many signatures an action needsWhich contracts, how much, until when
Typical walletExtension and seed phraseNido: nothing to install

Nido gives each of your users a C-address.

  • If you're new to Stellar, one thing first: Stellar has two kinds of account.
  • A G-address is an account with keys: one, or up to twenty with weights and thresholds. If you've used Ethereum, think of an externally owned account with multisig built in.
  • It can limit how many signatures an action needs, but not "this app may spend two XLM a day." The usual wallet is an extension and a seed phrase.
  • A C-address is a contract. Its code decides who can sign, which apps can act for it, which contracts they can call, how much they can spend, and until when. On Ethereum you'd call that a smart contract wallet.
  • Nido gives each of your users a C-address, behind one passkey.

About 50s.

Sources: developers.stellar.org/docs/learn/fundamentals/transactions/signatures-multisig, developers.stellar.org/docs/build/guides/contract-accounts

The old way vs with Nido

Getting in

The old way: a wallet extension
  • Install an extension
  • Create a password
  • Write down 12 words
  • Switch the network
  • Fund the account
With Nido: one passkey
  • Face ID or a fingerprint
  • Nothing to write down
  • Nothing to install
  • Or any key type, e.g. post-quantum
  • Recovery: add a trusted friend to get back in

Freighter screen: illustrative mock from the template walkthrough

  • Here's what that changes, starting with getting in.
  • The old way, a new user installs an extension, creates a password, writes down twelve words, switches network, and funds the account. Every step is a place people drop off.
  • With Nido, it's one passkey: Face ID or a fingerprint. Nothing to write down, and on testnet the account arrives with five test XLM.

About 45s.

Never locked out

Recovery

Off by default. Turn it on and choose:

Protect againstA lost passkey, or a stolen one
Who helpsTrusted friends, your recovery kit, or both
How manyFriends who must approve
TimingStandard: wait 7 days, then 14 days to finish
  • And if the user loses that passkey? Recovery is off until they turn it on.
  • They choose: a lost or a stolen passkey; trusted friends, a recovery kit, or both; how many friends must approve. Then a wait: seven days, then fourteen to finish.

About 25s.

The old way vs with Nido

Approve once, then no redirects

The old way: every signature goes to the wallet

1

trip to the wallet per guess, to read and confirm

With Nido: approve the app once

0

redirects per guess after that: the app’s session key signs

Approve in Nido · 1 passkey tapGuessGuessGuess …

Freighter screen: illustrative mock from the template walkthrough

  • Next, signing.
  • With a classic wallet, every signature sends the user to the wallet to read and confirm. In Guess the Number, that's one trip per guess.
  • With Nido, the user approves your app once, in Nido: one passkey tap for this sample. After that, signing never redirects: the app's session key signs each guess, and it just goes through.

About 45s.

The old way vs with Nido

Limits

The old way: no limit

The wallet signs whatever the user confirms. The only protection is reading every popup.

With Nido: a scoped key with a cap

The user approves a key for your app, and sets how much it can spend.

Spending capAn amount per day, week or month
ExpiryThe key stops working after it
Enforced byThe account, on chain

A call over the cap is refused before anything is sent.

  • And limits. A classic wallet signs whatever the user confirms, so the only protection is reading every popup.
  • With Nido, the scoped key for your app carries a spending cap, an amount per day, week or month, and an expiry.
  • The account enforces both, on chain. If your app, or anyone with its key, tries to spend past the cap, the call is refused before anything is sent.
  • That's the screenshot: the game at its 2 XLM a day cap. The guess stopped before the device was asked, and it cost nothing.

  • So, what Nido gives you.
  • For your users: no extension, no seed phrase. They approve an app once, and every approval has a cap and an expiry.
  • For your app: users signed in within a minute, with test XLM. Calls without popups. And limits that the account enforces, so you don't have to write them yourself.
  • That's the what. Now the how.

About 1 min.

Part 2

How to Nido

The same Scaffold React app and Guess the Number sample. Three diffs.


stellar scaffold init my-app \
    --template nidohq/scaffold-template
npm run tools:scaffold && npm ci && npm run doctor
npm run clients:testnet && npm run dev

1 · Imports    2 · Ask for access    3 · Call for the user

  • Start from the Nido template, a community template for Scaffold Stellar: stellar scaffold init, with nidohq slash scaffold-template.
  • Install, run doctor, build the clients, start the dev server. Same Scaffold React app, same Guess the Number sample. Three diffs against the default template.

About 30s.

Sources: github.com/nidohq/scaffold-template (NIDO.md, README.md), github.com/nidohq/scaffold-template/pull/10 (UX walkthrough), stellarscaffold.org/docs/community-templates

Diff 1 of 3 · vs the React template

Imports

app/src/components/GuessTheNumber.tsx

+import {
+  describe, isOverCap, submitCall,
+  xlmTokenId, type Grant,
+} from "@stellar-scaffold/app-lib"
 import { guessTheNumber } from
   "@stellar-scaffold/app-lib/clients"
 import { useState } from "react"
 import { useWallet } from "../hooks/useWallet"
+import { SessionGate } from "./SessionGate"

submitCall
Sends a call for any wallet

Grant, SessionGate
What the app asks the user for

xlmTokenId
The token to put a cap on

describe, isOverCap
Refusals as sentences

Nido’s wallet module is already in app-lib/wallet.ts. You don’t touch it.

  • Diff one: the imports. submitCall sends a call for any wallet; Grant and SessionGate describe what your app asks for; xlmTokenId lets you cap XLM; describe and isOverCap turn refusals into sentences.
  • Nido's wallet module is already wired into app-lib. You don't touch it.

About 35s.

Diff 2 of 3 · vs the React template

Connect, then ask for access

Connect · unchanged

Same connectWallet(). Nido is first in the picker.

GuessTheNumber.tsx

+const grants: Grant[] = [
+  { target: guessTheNumber.options.contractId,
+    functions: ["guess"],
+    duration: "24h", label: "guess" },
+  { target: xlmTokenId,
+    functions: ["transfer"], duration: "24h",
+    limit: { amount: "2", period: "day" },
+    label: "guess-xlm" },
+]
 …
+<SessionGate grants={grants} explain={…}>
   <form action={submitGuess}>…</form>
+</SessionGate>

One grant per contract the call touches. The user approves them once, in Nido.

  • Diff two. Connecting doesn't change: same connectWallet, and Nido is first in the picker.
  • What's new is grants, one per contract the call touches. A guess calls the game, and the game moves XLM, so two: the game's guess, and XLM transfer capped at two XLM a day. Both last twenty-four hours.
  • Wrap the form in a SessionGate with those grants. The user approves them once, in Nido, and the gate opens.

About 55s.

Diff 2 of 3 · what the user sees

The grants, in Nido

In your codeOn Nido’s page
target: guessTheNumberRule 1 · guess: only guess() on the game
target: xlmTokenIdRule 2 · guess-xlm: only transfer(), and only to the game
limit: 2 / dayThe cap. The user can change it before approving.
duration: "24h"Expires at a ledger about 24 hours away
your app’s keyThe session key: the app holds it, and it signs every guess

One passkey confirmation, and the SessionGate opens.

  • This is Nido's approval page. Each grant becomes a rule: rule one, only guess on the game; rule two, only XLM transfer, and Nido narrows it to paying the game.
  • Two XLM a day is the cap, which the user can change. Twenty-four hours becomes an expiry ledger. The app's key at the bottom is the session key that signs every guess.
  • One passkey confirmation, and the gate opens.

About 35s.

Sources: github.com/nidohq/scaffold-template/pull/10 (UX walkthrough)

Diff 3 of 3 · vs the React template

Call for the user

GuessTheNumber.tsx · submitGuess

-const tx = await guessTheNumber.guess(
-  { a_number: BigInt(guess), guesser: address },
-  { publicKey: address },
-)
-const { result } = await tx.signAndSend({ signTransaction })
+const { result, hash } = await submitCall(
+  address, (publicKey) =>
+    guessTheNumber.guess(
+      { a_number: BigInt(guess), guesser: address },
+      { publicKey })
+)

No new round-trip through Nido.

The app’s session key signs each call itself, and the account checks it against the grants.

A classic G-address wallet still works: submitCall signs with it as before.

  • Diff three. Before, you build the transaction with the user's address, then sign and send it with the wallet. That's the popup.
  • After, it's one submitCall, with the address and a function that builds the same guess.
  • No new round-trip through Nido: the app's session key signs each call, and the account checks it against the grants. A classic G-address wallet still signs the old way.
  • The passkey still matters for sign-in: that's the 1Password prompt for the Guess the Number app.

About 50s.

After approval · what your account enforces

Your policies, in plain words

Home: every policy change is in Recent activity
Account policy: the document, verified
  • Once approved, the grants are rules on the account. Home shows "Updated policies, 2 rules added" in Recent activity.
  • The Account policy page: 3 rules installed, the document verified against the hash on chain, and two signers: "admin", the user's passkey, with full authority, and "session", the app's key.

About 35s.

Same policy, two views

The policy, read and raw

The raw Perch policy document

{ "network": "Test SDF Network ; September 2015",
  "rules": [
    { "name": "admin", …, "scope": { "type": "self-admin" } },
    { "functions": ["guess"], "name": "guess", … },
    { "args": [{ "index": 1, "pred": {
        "address": "CBY4S4…ECYGUW", "type": "address-eq" } }],
      "cap": { "limit": "20000000", "period-ledgers": 17280 },
      "functions": ["transfer"],
      "name": "guess-xlm",
      "not-after-ledger": 5382692,
      "principals": { "signers": ["session"], "type": "all" },
      "scope": { "address": "CDLZFC…HGCYSC", "type": "contract" } }
  ],
  "signers": [{ "id": "admin", … }, { "id": "session", … }],
  "version": 1 }

Amounts are in stroops, 10,000,000 to the XLM. The account stores this document’s hash on chain.

  • The same policy both ways. On the left, Nido's card for guess-xlm: "session" can call transfer on the XLM contract, up to 2 XLM per day, until ledger 5382692.
  • On the right, the raw Perch policy document, Perch being the policy language Nido accounts enforce. Click through: three rules, admin, guess and guess-xlm, and two signers, admin and session.
  • guess-xlm in full. args: it can only pay the game. cap: 20000000 stroops is 2 XLM, and 17280 ledgers at about five seconds each is a day. not-after-ledger is the expiry.
  • The account stores the document's hash on chain, so what you read here is exactly what it enforces.

About 5 min, with questions.

Likely questions:

  • Mainnet? Hosted Nido is testnet-only today.
  • Who pays fees? Nido's relayer pays for account creation and grants. The app's session key pays each call's fee; on testnet Friendbot funds it, on mainnet the app would have to.
  • Where does the session key live? In the browser's localStorage for the app's origin. It never holds the user's funds; whoever reads it can spend at most the cap until the grants expire.
  • Revoking? Not in Nido yet; grants end at their expiry.
  • Why only one confirmation for two grants? One approval installs the session key plus all its rules, both grants, at once.
